Why the starting point deserves a page
changes what the untrained model does with its input and its output. This page measures each of these on the two real models.

vector. Sections G and H give the pros and cons and check the usual claims.

C · The range of random values each matrix gets
Xavier uniform: every number drawn evenly from −a to +a,
Same formula, different shapes, different ranges

Xavier picks a range from a matrix’s two dimensions, so that at the start a layer’s outputs are roughly the same size as its inputs. It works well for a matrix that multiplies vectors. For an embedding table, one of the "dimensions" is simply the number of tokens in the
, so the range ends up depending on how big the

sequence A · length of the token part (
Which half of the input vector is louder
Every input vector is the sum of two parts: the token’s embedding row, multiplied by √
), and the positional encoding of its position (
). The positional encoding always has length
, in both versions. The token part’s length depends on the embedding range from section C — so the two versions start with the balance
between "which word" and "which position" the other way round.
What to take from section D
the untrained model mostly "hears" where a token is: the position part is
longer than the token part, so two different words at the same position start out with very similar input vectors. In
it mostly hears which token it is: the token part is about twice the position part. Neither is wrong — training adjusts the embedding
table either way — but it is a real difference in the first forward pass that nobody chose on purpose: it falls out of the

A fair "I don’t know" against a confident wrong answer
’s output head is its own random matrix with the tiny ±
range, and it has nothing to do with the embeddings.
’s output head IS the embedding table (weight tying), with the wide ±
range. The score of a token is then the decoder’s output (length ≈
) multiplied with that token’s own embedding row.
Before any training, the decoder’s output at a position still looks a lot like the embedding of the token it is reading — so that token gets a huge score.

is cleaner almost everywhere — with one surprising cost

Most of the differences are straightforward improvements. The one that is not is section E: the tied head with a wide range makes the untrained model confidently wrong, which training fixes within a few epochs.

halves the parameter count by deleting

tables, not by shrinking the model: the layers that process a sentence actually grow. It creates its weights more carefully — each matrix drawn once, the padding vector really zero, the same weights on every run. The one side effect is that, with a small
output head, the untrained model starts out confidently predicting the token it is reading, so its first loss (
) is far above an even guess — and training removes that within the first twenty epochs.
